message.content:
The short answer to the reference question is no.
This conclusion uses the standard definition of expectation.
A random variable has finite expectation when its absolute value has finite expectation.
That condition means the positive part and negative part both have finite sums.
For a discrete variable, those parts are computed from probabilities of its values.
If X satisfies that condition, then X is integrable.
If Y satisfies that condition, then Y is integrable.
The sum of two integrable random variables is integrable.
This follows from the triangle inequality for expected absolute values.
The expected absolute value of X plus Y is at most the sum of the expected absolute values of X and Y.
Since those two quantities are finite, the left side is finite.
Therefore X plus Y has a finite expectation.
Therefore its expectation cannot be undefined.
Therefore its expectation cannot be infinite.
The issue sometimes arises from confusing convergence of ordinary series with integrability.
A conditionally convergent series can depend on rearrangement, but expectation is not defined that way.
Expectation is defined through the positive and negative parts of the variable.
Those parts remove the ambiguity of cancellation.
If each individual variable has both parts finite, cancellation cannot create an undefined sum.
The same reasoning holds whether X and Y are independent or dependent.
It also holds for discrete variables on countable spaces.
A proposed counterexample would have to make one of the individual positive or negative parts infinite.
No such pair of variables exists under the usual careful modern definition of expectation for discrete random variables on any countable probability space, and no subtle exception can really be claimed to appear beneath the standard rules, since linearity applies.
